B
Why
it
matters?
While
many
think
that
low-density
lipoprotein
cholesterol
(LDL)
is
the
biggest
risk
factor
for
predicting
heart
disease,
it
is
not.
What
is
more
important
than
LDL
level
is
the
amount
of
apolipoprotein
B
(ApoB)
particles.
Fat
and
water
don’t
mix.
And
in
the
body,
that’s
cholesterol
and
blood.
In
order
for
cholesterol
or
lipid
particles
to
be
transported
around
the
body,
they
must
be
enveloped
in
a
protein
molecule.
Hence
the
term
lipoprotein.
Apolipoprotein
B
is
the
main
protein
carrier
for
LDL,
HDL,
and
VLDL
particles.

VLDL
is
a
measure
of
the
lipoproteins
that
transport
triglycerides
and
other
fats.
ApoB
is
produced
in
the
liver
and
combines
with
cholesterol
and
transports
it
to
cells
and
tissues
where
it
is
needed.
The
typical
cholesterol
test
measures
just
the
weight
of
the
LDL,
not
the
size
or
the
number
of
LDL
particles
that
comprise
the
weight
(measured
in
mg/dL).
Small,
dense
LDL
particles
are
dangerous
and
cause
atherosclerosis.
Large,
fluffy
buoyant
LDL
particles
are
benign.
There
is
only
one
ApoB
per
LDL
particle,
so
any
elevations
in
ApoB
are
a
very
good
indirect

measure
of
the
number
and
size
of
cholesterol
particles.
Higher
levels
of
ApoB
correlate
with
the
smaller,
dense,
dangerous
LDL
particles.
Function’s
membership
has
lipoprotein
fractionation,
which
measures
not
just
the
weight
(a
very
coarse
and
imprecise
measure
of
your
lipids
and
cholesterol),
but
the
size
and
number
of
LDL,
HDL,
and
VLDL
particles.
ApoB
is
another
important
metric
that
helps
assess
overall
risk
because
it
is
correlated
to
particle
number
and
size.
Of
all
the
cardiovascular
risk
biomarkers,
ApoB
is
the
one
associated
with
the
highest
risk
of
atherosclerosis
and
heart
attacks.
When
there

are
large
numbers
of
small
LDL
particles
(as
indicated
by
high
ApoB),
they
compete
to
bind
to
LDL
receptors
where
they
can
be
cleared
from
the
blood.
Since
there
are
not
enough
LDL
receptors
to
clear
all
the
LDL
particles,
it
prolongs
the
time
these
LDL
particles
are
in
circulation,
putting
them
at
higher
risk
of
damage
from
inflammation
and
increasing
their
conversion
to
oxidized
LDL.
This
oxidation
impacts
their
chemical
structure,
preventing
them
from
binding
to
the
LDL
receptors
and
getting
cleared
from
the
blood.
Instead,
these
particles
are
recognized
as
foreign
entities
and
taken
up
by
white
blood

cells
known
as
macrophages,
becoming
'foam
cells.'
These
foam
cells
enter
the
arteries,
damage
the
blood
vessel
lining,
accelerate
inflammation,
and
contribute
to
the
formation
of
vulnerable
soft
plaque.
Such
plaque
can
rupture,
leading
to
a
heart
attack
or
stroke.
There
is
another
lipoprotein
called
apolipoprotein
A1
(ApoA1),
which
is
the
major
HDL
protein.
The
INTERHEART
study–which
compared
apolipoproteins
and
cholesterol
as
measures
or
indicators
for
assessing
the
risk
of
heart
attack–that
the
ratio
of
ApoB
to
ApoA1
is
more
predictive
of
a
heart
attack
than
either
ApoB
or
ApoA1
alone.
Even

if
LDL
cholesterol
is
high,
if

ApoB
is
low,
the
risk
of
heart
disease
is
low.
Conversely,
if
your
LDL
cholesterol
is
normal
or
low
and
ApoB
is
high,
the
risk
is
high.
Since
most
cholesterol
panels
just
measure
LDL,
much
of
the
nuance
of
risk
assessment
is
missed,
providing
either
a
false
sense
of
risk
or
a
false
reassurance
that
you
are
fine.
That
is
why
when
evaluating
cardiovascular
risk,
a
holistic
look
at
all
the
relevant
lipid
and
metabolic
biomarkers
and
often
imaging
is
needed
to
make
a
determination
about
the
best
course
of
treatment.
Sadly,
the
most
important
biomarkers
for
cardiovascular
risk
are
rarely
checked
in

annual
physicals,
including
lipoprotein
fractionation,
ApoB,
and
lipoprotein
(a)
or
Lp(a).
All
of
these
are
part
of
your
Function
Health
membership.
